title: CRDTs, and the libraries that implement them

videos.script:
Two lessons asked what to do when two copies disagree. This one changes the question. {{shape}} What if the data were shaped so that every disagreement had an answer written down in advance?

That is a CRDT. Its copies merge in any order, as often as you like, and always reach the same state. {{orders}}

You build two by hand. {{counter}} A counter where the phone's thirty minutes and the tablet's forty-five both count. {{set}} And a set where one device adds a tag while the other removes a different one, and both stick.

Then you hand the hard case to a library. {{yjs}} Yjs merges the planner's week, field by field, note by note.

And you weigh what it costs. {{bytes}} A thousand edits, and the history can outweigh the data many times over. A CRDT promises agreement. It does not promise that what everyone agrees on is what anybody meant.
